articles.title: Japanese intellectuals warn against country's return to "prewar state"
articles.body:
TOKYO, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- Japanese intellectuals and citizens have warned against the country's return to a "prewar state," voicing concern over Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's policies to expand Japan's military capabilities and ease restrictions on arms exports.
The remarks were made Thursday evening at a symposium in Tokyo themed "Do Not Let Japan Move Toward a New Prewar State," where participants examined the risks posed by the Takaichi administration's defense policies and called on Japan to avoid repeating the mistakes of war.
In April, the Takaichi government revised the "three principles on transfer of defense equipment and technology," lifting a ban on exports of lethal weapons. It also plans to revise the country's three key security documents by the end of this year.
Japanese media have recently reported that the government may alter the wording of the country's Three Non-Nuclear Principles during the revision and consider including discussions on the introduction of nuclear-powered submarines.
Atsushi Koketsu, professor emeritus at Yamaguchi University, outlined how Japan has gradually relaxed restrictions on arms exports. Although the three security documents have yet to be revised, he said Japan's 2026 Defense White Paper and other policy documents suggest that the revision will further promote military buildup and strengthen the country's defense industry.
Koketsu told Xinhua that the policies and ideology of the Takaichi administration bear a striking resemblance to those of the Japanese militarist regime of the 1930s. He asserted that Takaichi's tenure must be brought to an end as soon as possible, and that a cabinet committed to the cause of peace should be established in its place.
Mizuho Fukushima, leader of Japan's Social Democratic Party, said she felt a strong sense of crisis over Japan's slide toward a "new prewar state." She noted that Japan's economy and military sector were becoming increasingly integrated and warned that the three security documents could be revised through a Cabinet decision after the current extraordinary Diet session concludes.
Mitsutaka Ito, a Japanese citizen who attended the symposium, told Xinhua that although the event's theme urged Japan not to move toward a new prewar state, many people believed the country was already in such a state. He described the planned revision of the three security documents as a highly dangerous development.
Takakage Fujita, secretary-general of the Association for Inheriting and Propagating the Murayama Statement, told Xinhua that lifting restrictions on lethal weapons exports and planning to revise the security documents were not isolated measures but part of the Takaichi government's broader military buildup, reflecting its right-wing orientation.
Fujita described Takaichi as a strongly right-wing advocate of military expansion among Japan's postwar prime ministers. He said her far-right nature is now being exposed in a particularly egregious manner, accusing her of distorting history, denying Japan's war of aggression, and continually expanding the country's military capabilities while catering to the United States.
Fujita called for Takaichi to leave office as soon as possible. ■

articles.title: Cambodia marks World Food Day 2026 with focus on agriculture innovation
articles.body:
PHNOM PENH, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- Cambodia on Friday celebrated World Food Day 2026 in the far northeastern province of Ratanakiri, aiming to raise awareness and inspire collective action toward food security, improved nutrition, and zero hunger, according to a news release from the Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries (MAFF).
Under the global theme "Innovate today. Nourish tomorrow," the event brought together government representatives, development partners, farmers, and Indigenous communities to highlight agricultural innovation, sustainable food production, and rural livelihoods.
Organized by MAFF in collaboration with the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) and the World Food Program (WFP), the celebration was attended by MAFF Secretary of State Keo Omalis, FAO Representative to Cambodia Rebekah Bell, and WFP Deputy Country Director Fumitsugu Tosu.
The celebration featured Indigenous cultural performances, traditional food demonstrations, agricultural exhibitions, the distribution of vegetable seeds and tree seedlings, and a symbolic tree-planting ceremony.
"The event aims to raise awareness and inspire a collective global spirit regarding the importance of ensuring food security and nutrition while combating hunger," Omalis said at the ceremony.
"The Royal Government's Pentagonal Strategy - Phase 1 places a strong focus on developing the agricultural sector, ensuring food and nutrition security, and promoting environmental sustainability," he added.
The official expressed high appreciation for the FAO, WFP, relevant partner organizations, inter-agency bodies, and sub-national administrations for their vital roles in providing food and nutritional support to vulnerable communities throughout Cambodia.
According to the news release, a special highlight of the event was the recognition of 10 outstanding women for their contributions to agriculture and rural development, marking the International Year of the Woman Farmer 2026. ■

articles.title: Across China: A young returnee's bet on the "sea of death"
articles.body:
CHENGDU, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- Luo Lan first came to Hongyuan in southwest China's Sichuan Province by chance, only to find that its landscape reminded her of Scotland, where she had studied.
In 2021, she visited the county with fellow alumni to do charity work. Having studied in Glasgow, Britain, she felt an immediate sense of familiarity. "And the locals were warm, sincere and honest," she recalled.
Located in Aba Tibetan and Qiang Autonomous Prefecture and established in the 1960s, Hongyuan County commemorates the Long March with its name, which literally means "the grasslands the Red Army crossed."
From 1935 to 1936, the Red Army climbed snow-capped mountains and crossed grasslands and swamps in what is now Hongyuan County, one of the Long March's most treacherous stretches.
The grasslands are often dubbed the "sea of death." "The perils of the grasslands were no surprise," wrote Harrison Salisbury in The Long March: The Untold Story. "Beneath the flowers lurked bogs that could swallow a man in a minute."
Today, Hongyuan is home to numerous monuments and memorial halls honoring the Red Army. To help local farmers and herdsmen boost their incomes, the county has also developed tourism around its vast grasslands.
Luo became part of that transformation.
One year after her first visit to Hongyuan, Luo, then working for a real estate company, saw an opportunity to develop a hotel featuring movable wooden cabins. "The houses are elevated on stilts to avoid damaging the pasture," she explained.
Starting with just five rooms, the hotel proved an immediate success, with bookings filling up throughout the travel season in its first year.
"This land attracts travelers from far and wide hoping to experience a slower pace of life," Luo said. "Away from the hustle and bustle of the city, they can feel the vastness and tranquility of the Hongyuan grassland, enjoy the wind, the starry sky and the sunset."
When her company later withdrew from the project, she refused to give up and launched her own business in 2023. Today, her homestay in Xiahalama Village has four two-story wooden cabins, four single-story cabins, two space capsule rooms and five steel-framed houses, hosting about 4,000 guests a year.
The homestay also offers a special "nomadic day tour" package. Guests milk yaks with herders, make butter tea in the morning, enjoy an authentic Tibetan breakfast, and ride horses through flower-strewn meadows in the afternoon. Bilingual local Tibetan guides lead the tours, offering visitors a firsthand experience of nomadic culture.
Next to the homestay, Luo also opened the "Chi Yun Qu" (Cloud-Eating) cafe, which blends Tibetan aesthetics with modern design and draws around 16,000 visitors annually. The signature "Butter Latte" combines Tibetan butter with Italian espresso, and the latte art features traditional Tibetan patterns.
Sonam Rizgin, a village cadre in Xiahalama, told Xinhua that visitors come not only from nearby areas in Sichuan and Chongqing, but also from elsewhere across China and even overseas. The peak season runs from May to October, with July and August the busiest months.
"Currently, 21 villagers work there, and students return to work part-time during school holidays," he said. Tourism generates about 400,000 yuan (about 59,799 U.S. dollars) in annual income for the village.
Hongyuan County was lifted out of poverty in 2020. Chen Zhimin, a county publicity official, noted that entrepreneurs from outside the area like Luo not only help raise villagers' incomes but also bring fresh ideas to local communities.
"For example, they bring new media communication skills, create immersive experiences of indigenous nomadic culture, and blend tradition with fashion," she said.
With such support, the county has hosted equestrian competitions and music festivals to promote itself as a tourist destination.
"Well-known singers perform at the music festivals. During these events, daily coffee sales can exceed 10,000 yuan, and accommodation is fully booked," Chen added.
Hongyuan is not the only place along the Long March route to emerge as a popular tourist destination.
Jiajin Mountain, the first major snow-capped mountain the Red Army crossed, has become a hiking destination for outdoor enthusiasts. As of August 2026, the Jiajin Mountain scenic area had recorded 13,327 tourist visits so far this year, up 1.45 percent year on year.
Songpan County, another area where the Red Army crossed the grasslands, received 10.64 million tourist visits in 2025, up 15.53 percent year on year, with total tourism spending reaching 31.81 billion yuan.
Improved infrastructure and better transport links have helped fuel this growth.
Aba, which covers 84,000 square kilometers, roughly the size of the island of Ireland, is connected to China's national rail network, providing access to major cities such as Chongqing, Xi'an, Beijing, Shanghai and Guangzhou.
Expressways are lined with gas stations and electric vehicle charging facilities. A journey from western Sichuan to Gansu that once took the Red Army months can now be completed by road and rail in a day, or in some cases, just a few hours.
The Aba grasslands are now served by two airports. Hongyuan Airport, which opened in 2014, is only an hour's drive from Luo's homestay.
"The altitude is high, and the temperature difference can reach 40 degrees Celsius. It starts hailing in September, so you can imagine how hard it was for the Red Army back then," Luo said. "But conditions are much better now. We have underfloor heating, access to all kinds of food, and we can even eat tropical fruits."
She acknowledges that her business is still finding its feet and faces challenges, including high energy costs. Yet compared with the hardships the Red Army endured, she remains optimistic.
In her cafe, Luo keeps a collection of books for guests to read, including several about the Long March.
Reflecting on the past, she said: "Today, we are enjoying peace and sitting here sipping coffee. Isn't this exactly what they hoped to see during the Long March?" ■

articles.title: China Focus: China, U.S. youth seek connection, cooperation via exchange program
articles.body:
BEIJING, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- For 16-year-old Otoota Uipi, who has studied Chinese for more than a decade and counts Chinese pop star Jay Chou among her favorite artists, visiting China for the first time fulfilled a long-held dream.
Already familiar with the Chinese language and pop culture, the U.S. teenager was still struck by technological innovations: hotel service robots, advanced university labs, and digital tools woven into ordinary life.
Gathering roughly 200 students from China and the United States, the Beijing trip earlier this week came amid a major expansion of bilateral people-to-people ties.
In November 2023, China announced a five-year initiative to invite 50,000 young Americans to China for exchange and study programs. The target was met two and a half years ahead of schedule earlier this year. It recently launched a new plan to invite 100,000 young Americans to visit China for exchange and study over the next five years.
The three-day event, co-hosted by the China Education Association for International Exchange and Peking University and designed to help young people move beyond stereotypes and connect directly across cultures, featured campus tours, cultural activities and roundtable talks.
Uipi explored university campuses with her Chinese peers, swapping stories about local food and everyday tech use. She called these conversations "an interesting experience."
Maria Sablan, a college student from Saipan in the U.S. Northern Mariana Islands, gained a new perspective on China. Accustomed to life in a quieter island community, she had worried China's bustling cities would overwhelm her. Those fears faded once she arrived.
"This exchange really helps us understand one another," Sablan said. She hopes to visit Chinese museums to learn history beyond textbooks.
Shared passions quickly bridged cultural gaps for some participants. Mo Jiaxin, a student at Renmin University of China, recalled how a casual mention of the Los Angeles Lakers sparked an energetic conversation with visiting Californian students.
"When we open our hearts and engage with sincerity, understanding and resonance come naturally," Mo said.
Kimball Schuenman, a middle school student from Utah, a western U.S. state, identified deeper common ground. Young people on both sides of the Pacific pursue quality education and fulfilling careers, while confronting shared global challenges: climate change and rapid AI-driven transformation. He views differing perspectives not as barriers, but as assets for solving those problems.
"We come from different countries with different trains of thought. If we come together, we'll be able to think of different solutions," Schuenman said.
The program also hosted structured, in-depth dialogue. At Tsinghua University, participants held three roundtable sessions on "Technology for Good: Innovation and Responsibility," debating how innovation can better serve human needs. Cao Ruoqi, a Tsinghua student, moderated a discussion on AI's evolving role in education and responsible AI use in classrooms.
"Such discussions enable young people from diverse cultural backgrounds and life experiences to inspire one another and gain insights hard to acquire from reading alone," Cao said. She noted one panel cannot resolve complex global problems overnight, yet exchanges like this can "sow a seed in the lives of young people from both countries" that might "grow into a forest of lasting friendship and future cooperation."
The Beijing gathering marks the latest step to revitalize China-U.S. youth exchanges. Wei Wei, a U.S. delegation team leader and Chinese teacher based in the United States, said American student demand for China travel continues to rise.
"I feel a sense of responsibility to promote greater youth exchanges between the two countries, and help more students become cultural ambassadors," Wei said. ■

articles.title: Iran's navy says another "violating" oil tanker caught fire east of Hormuz Strait
articles.body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- The Iranian Army's Navy announced on Friday that its forces detected another "violating" oil tanker that had caught fire east of the Strait of Hormuz.
In a statement on its website, the navy said the tanker was spotted by its monitoring teams, "which are responsible for the continuous control of the strait's eastern waters," in the waterway's "forbidden region."
It added that the vessel had turned off its tracking systems and was seeking to cross the "forbidden region," stressing that such "uncoordinated movements" cause insecurity and hazards for other vessels.
On Tuesday and Thursday, the navy announced it had detected two other "violating" oil tankers that caught fire while attempting to cross the "forbidden region" east of the strait.
It emphasized that its forces have full control and dominance over the strait's eastern waters and are continuously monitoring all "enemy" activities and vessel movements in real time.
The navy strongly advised all vessels to strictly refrain from switching off their electronic equipment in compliance with international regulations and to ensure necessary coordination with Iran's armed forces for safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran tightened its grip on the strait on Feb. 28, barring safe passage of vessels belonging to or affiliated with Israel and the United States following their joint strikes on Iranian territory. ■

articles.title: Celadon industry upgraded in Longquan, China's Zhejiang
articles.body:
A staff member livestreams at a studio of the Longquan celadon in Longquan, east China's Zhejiang Province, Oct. 14, 2026. Located in southwestern Zhejiang Province, Longquan City boasts abundant ceramic clay, dense forests, and the Longquan River, providing ideal conditions for its celadon industry.
Longquan celadon firing technique was listed as a national intangible cultural heritage in 2006 and was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2009.
In recent years, Longquan has upgraded its celadon industry by improving the quality of raw material, boosting industrial intelligence and empowering innovation. Today, the city has over 3,000 celadon-related businesses with more than 23,000 workers involved. (Xinhua/Jiang Han)
